vignette:
Nadia was 51, a divorced Middle Eastern woman who had spent most of her adult life trying to build something steady and useful for others. She worked in social ministry, often moving between offices, community spaces, and home visits, and she was the sort of person colleagues described as dependable and calm. In sessions, though, she described a childhood that had never felt safe in the ordinary way other people seemed to mean by that word. As a girl she had been physically abused by a caregiver, and what remained with her was not a single scene but a set of bodily and emotional impressions that still arrived with force decades later. When she tried to talk about what happened, she said she could not seem to put it into words; the events felt known in her body more than in language.

She remembered one episode in particular with a harsh clarity that made sense of why certain situations now felt so charged. She was a child, trapped in a room with the caregiver, the space feeling too small and the adult too close. In later recounting, she described not just fear but the sensation that her body had gone back to that exact posture—fixed, braced, as if she were still in the same position while the frightening event was happening. That bodily memory came back especially when she felt cornered or when someone stood between her and a way out. Even in the present, if she was in a meeting or at a home visit, she automatically placed herself near the door. She made sure she knew where the exit was and could leave quickly if she needed to, and over time this became a habit she barely noticed until she described it in detail. She also took care never to be alone with another person if she could help it. At work, she was careful to keep conversations in open spaces, to ask for another staff member to join her, or to make sure a door remained open. She did not frame this as suspiciousness so much as caution; being alone with someone felt, to her, like removing the one thing that might protect her if a situation changed suddenly.

Her days were often organized around scanning for danger. She said she frequently looked behind her to check whether someone was following her, especially when walking to her car after work or moving through a hallway in a ministry building. Sometimes the feeling would arrive before she had any clear reason for it. A person behind her, a footstep echoing in a corridor, or even a sudden silence could make her react as if something was wrong. She described these moments as false alarms, but they were still immediate and physical, with her body already preparing before her mind had caught up. In those moments she became irritable and could snap at others more quickly than she intended, sometimes with angry outbursts that surprised even her. She was embarrassed by this because it felt so unlike the composed role she tried to maintain in her work and in her family relationships, yet she also experienced the anger as familiar, as though it belonged to the same old history of being hurt and having to endure it.

As the years passed, these patterns shaped her life in quieter but consequential ways. She began avoiding going to work or study when she could, especially on days when she anticipated being around unfamiliar people or confined in spaces where she could not easily position herself near a door. Because her job involved helping others, this avoidance was painful and conflicted; she valued the ministry deeply, but some mornings she sat in her car outside the office long enough to feel her own reluctance and dread become almost tangible. She had built a life around service, yet she found herself shrinking from the very settings where service happened. The consequence was that she sometimes arrived late, declined certain assignments, or arranged her schedule to reduce the amount of time she spent in enclosed rooms or one-on-one situations. She had become increasingly aware that these adjustments were narrowing her world.

Nadia sought help when she realized the pattern was no longer something she could simply work around. The combination of constant watchfulness, the need to position herself by exits, the refusal to be alone with others, and the abrupt anger had become exhausting. She feared that one day her body would react in a way she could not manage in front of a colleague or client, or that she would miss an important part of her work because she was too busy checking behind her or calculating how to leave. More than anything, she hoped to feel less haunted by the old scenes that still lived in her body without words, and to move through her work and daily life without feeling as though danger could appear at any moment.
